Conventions

Method names are listed exactly as implemented.
Signatures are shown in Nex-style pseudocode.
nil means no useful return value.
Some behavior differs by runtime (jvm vs node), especially for Process and platform-specific libraries under lib/.

Waits for the first task in tasks to complete and returns its result.

title: Built-in Functions

text:
Real
Real literals must include at least one digit after the decimal point. Valid forms include 3.14 , 10.0 , .5 , and 12.0e-3 . Forms such as 10. and 12.e-3 are not valid real literals.
Real is an IEEE-754 double on every backend, in representation and arithmetic. Division by zero follows IEEE rather than raising: 1.0 / 0.0 is Infinity , -1.0 / 0.0 is -Infinity , and 0.0 / 0.0 is NaN . (Integer division by zero, by contrast, raises.)

truncate none Integer The value with its fraction dropped (toward zero). Raises as floor does.

The math methods follow IEEE-754 as division does: outside a function's domain the result is NaN or an infinity, not an error. (-1.0).sqrt and 2.0.asin are NaN , 0.0.log is -Infinity . title: Collection Types
text:
Array
This section covers the standard collection abstractions used throughout Nex code. Array, Map, Set, and Min_Heap[T] are built-in collection types. Stack[T] is a common generic collection class pattern built on top of Array[T].
All built-in collection types inherit Any. Their to_string, equals, and clone methods operate recursively: to_string renders nested structure, equals performs deep structural equality, and clone performs a deep copy.

Construction
create Min_Heap.empty
create Min_Heap[Integer].empty

create Min_Heap.empty creates an empty heap that uses natural ordering.
empty() is intended for element types that already support ordering: built-in sortable scalars or classes implementing Comparable.
For non-Comparable element types, use from_comparator(...).

text:
Stack[T]
Stack[T] is a generic last-in, first-out collection abstraction. It is not a built-in primitive type; it is typically defined as a class using Array[T] for storage.

Typical Definition
class Stack [T]
  create
    make() do
      items := []
    end

  feature
    items: Array[T]

    push(value: T) do
      items.add(value)
    end

    pop(): T do
      result := items.get(items.length - 1)
      items.remove(items.length - 1)
    end

    peek(): T do
      result := items.get(items.length - 1)
    end

    is_empty(): Boolean do
      result := items.is_empty
    end

    size(): Integer do
      result := items.length
    end
end


Methods

Arguments
Returns
Description

value: T
Void
Push value onto the top of the stack.

Notes

pop and peek usually require the stack to be non-empty.
A contract-based version should add preconditions for these operations.
Stack[T] is the canonical example of a user-defined generic collection in Nex.

let xs: Array [Integer] := [10, 20]
xs.add(30)
xs.add_at(1, 15)                  -- [10, 15, 20, 30]

m.set("kind", "language")
print(m.get("lang"))              -- "Nex"

stack.push(10)
stack.push(20)
print(stack.peek)                 -- 20

title: Exception Classes
text:
When the language itself raises an exception — a failed contract,
integer division by zero, an index out of range, and so on — the value a
rescue block receives in exception is an
object of one of the classes below, chosen by the kind of failure. A
handler can therefore tell failures apart with convert or
match instead of reading a message.

A value raised with raise is not
wrapped: raise "transient" still hands the handler the
string "transient", and raise 42 the integer
42.

These classes are defined in lib/lang/exception.nex
(Definition of Nex, Appendix B.7).

title: Exception Classes
text:
Loading

A program that has a rescue anywhere, or that names one
of these classes, gets the library automatically, as if it had
written:

intern lang/Exception

Writing that intern yourself also works.

A program that declares a class of its own with one of these names
does not get the library. Its handlers then receive the failure's
message as a String, as they did before the classes
existed.

title: Exception Classes
text:
Handling exceptions

Test for a class with convert:

do
  account.withdraw(500.0)
rescue
  if convert exception to v: Precondition_Violation then
    print("refused: " + v.message)     -- refused: Precondition violation: enough
  else
    raise exception                    -- not ours: pass it on
  end
end

Or dispatch with match (exception has type
Any, so give an else):

do
  print(totals.get(i) / count)
rescue
  match exception of
    Division_by_Zero then print("no items")
    Index_Out_Of_Bounds as e then print("bad index: " + e.message)
  else
    raise exception
  end
end

A contract violation's label says which assertion failed:

rescue
  if convert exception to c: Contract_Violation then
    if ?c.label as l then print("failed: " + l) end
  end

Re-raising a caught exception with raise exception
reports its message if nothing else catches it.

title: Exception Classes
text:
Defining your own

Inherit Exception, delegate to its constructor, and
raise an instance:

class Parse_Error
inherit Exception
create
  make(m: String) do
    Exception.make(m)
  end
end

do
  raise create Parse_Error.make("unexpected token")
rescue
  if convert exception to p: Parse_Error then
    print("parse failed: " + p.message)
  end
end

An uncaught one is reported through its to_string:
Error: unexpected token.

title: Exception Classes
text:
Notes

print(exception) for a built-in failure prints the
message without quotes, because exception is an object, not
a string.

exception is typed Any in a
rescue block, since raise accepts any value;
narrow it with convert or match to reach
message, label or
host_class.

On the tree-walking interpreter (--interpret),
unbounded recursion stops the interpreter itself rather than raising a
catchable Host_Exception.

title: Audio Libraries
text:
Without a sound device
When there is no sound device, or the environment variable NEX_AUDIO (or the Java system property nex.audio ) is off , every audio class still works but plays nothing:
Sound still loads, knows its length and counts play_count .
Synth still keeps each channel's instrument and counts notes_played .
Music and Midi_Song still move through their states. A Midi_Song 's sequencer keeps running in real time, so it reaches its end as usual; a Music stays at position 0 and never reaches its end by itself.
is_audible() reports false .
A test can therefore drive a program headless and check which sounds it asked for — say, that the hit sound played three times.

title: Audio Libraries
text:
Files
Sound and Music read WAV, AIFF and AU files with uncompressed (PCM) audio; MP3 and OGG are not supported. Midi_Song reads standard MIDI files. A relative file name is resolved against the directory nex was started from ( NEX_USER_DIR ), as in Picture.load .

title: Audio Libraries
text:
Track
The deferred class behind Music and Midi_Song : something that plays over time, with the state machine below. Every contract here is inherited.
play pause STOPPED ──► PLAYING ───────► PAUSED ▲ │ ▲ resume │ └── stop ──┘ └─────────────┘ (stop from PAUSED too)
The state changes only on the program's calls. The audio itself runs on a background thread, so a track can reach its end at any moment. That shows at once in reached_end() , and the state follows it when update() is called — a game calls it once per frame:
music.update() if music.is_stopped() then next_level_music.play() end
This is what lets play() promise is_playing() : nothing can change the state between the routine's body and the postcondition check.

A piece of music written in code, note by note. Time is counted in ticks, and a beat is ticks_per_beat ticks; a song plays at 120 beats per minute unless Midi_Song.set_tempo says otherwise.

title: Graphics Libraries
text:
Canvas
A Canvas draws in user coordinates onto an offscreen image, and shows that image in a window on request.
Coordinates. (0, 0) is the bottom left and (1, 1) the top right until set_x_scale / set_y_scale change them. y grows upward.
Centre-based shapes. circle(x, y, radius) , square(x, y, half_side) and rectangle(x, y, half_width, half_height) are all centred on (x, y). Lengths are scaled per axis, so with unequal x and y scales a circle comes out as an ellipse.
Pen. Lines and outlines are drawn with the pen color, 2 * pen_radius pixels wide. The pen radius is in pixels, not user units. Colors with an alpha below 255 blend with what is underneath.
Window. show copies the offscreen image to the window, opening the window the first time. A canvas that never calls show never opens one. Without a display, show only updates the onscreen image and wait_until_closed returns at once, so the same program runs headless.
Buffering. With double buffering off (the default), every drawing command also refreshes an already open window. With it on, the window changes only on show . Turn it on for flicker-free animation.
Program exit. The window closes when the program ends. A script that should stay on screen ends with wait_until_closed() .
File names. A relative name given to save or Picture.load is resolved against the directory nex was started from ( NEX_USER_DIR ), not the Nex install directory the launcher runs in.

title: Graphics Libraries
text:
Input
While the window is open, the mouse and keyboard are polled, as in StdDraw. A program reads them once per pass through its loop:
from until c.is_key_pressed(Key.ESCAPE) or not c.is_window_open() do if c.is_mouse_pressed() then c.filled_circle(c.mouse_x(), c.mouse_y(), 0.01) end c.pause(16) end Feature Returns Description has_mouse_position() Boolean Whether the mouse has been over the window yet. mouse_x() , mouse_y() Real Where the mouse was last seen over the window, in user coordinates. Require has_mouse_position() . is_mouse_pressed() Boolean Whether a mouse button is held down. has_next_key_typed() Boolean Whether a typed character is waiting. next_key_typed() String The oldest typed character not read yet, as a one-character string, removed from the queue. Requires has_next_key_typed() . is_key_pressed(code: Integer) Boolean Whether the key with this code is held down. Use the Key constants. Typed characters are what the keyboard produced ( "A" with Shift held, "a" without). Held keys are physical keys ( Key.A either way, Key.LEFT , Key.SHIFT ). Keys and buttons held when the window loses focus count as released, since their release would never be heard.
Keyboard input goes to the window that has focus. A new window normally gets it. If it doesn't, click it.

title: Graphics Libraries
text:
Pictures
Load a Picture once and draw it as often as needed. A PNG's transparency is kept, so a sprite with a transparent background draws cleanly over the scene. Pictures are always drawn fully opaque, whatever the pen's alpha.
let ship := create Picture.load("ship.png") c.enable_double_buffering() from until c.is_key_pressed(Key.ESCAPE) or not c.is_window_open() do if c.is_key_pressed(Key.LEFT) then heading := heading + 4.0 end if c.is_mouse_pressed() then x := c.mouse_x() y := c.mouse_y() end c.clear() c.picture(x, y, ship, 0.05, 0.05, heading) c.show() c.pause(16) end To tell whether the mouse is over a picture, compare mouse_x / mouse_y with where you drew it, for example (c.mouse_x() - x).hypot(c.mouse_y() - y) < r .

The state behind a canvas's input queries, in pixels (0, 0 at the top left). The window feeds it from Swing's event thread, so it is safe to read while events arrive. It can also be fed directly, to test input handling without a window or to replay a scripted session:
c.input.record_mouse_button(40, 60, true) -- pixel (40, 60), button down c.input.record_key_typed("q") c.input.record_key(Key.LEFT, true) -- LEFT held Feature Description record_mouse_moved(px, py: Integer) The mouse is at pixel (px, py). record_mouse_button(px, py: Integer, is_down: Boolean) A button went down or up at (px, py). record_key_typed(s: String) A character was typed. Requires a one-character s . record_key(code: Integer, is_down: Boolean) A key went down or up. release_all() Forget held keys and buttons. has_mouse_position() , mouse_px() , mouse_py() , is_mouse_pressed() , has_next_key_typed() , next_key_typed() , is_key_pressed(code) As on Canvas , with positions in pixels. It also implements java.awt.event.MouseListener , MouseMotionListener , KeyListener and WindowFocusListener , which is how the window feeds it.

Picture
An image in memory: read from a PNG, JPEG, GIF or BMP file, or made blank, then read and changed pixel by pixel, transformed, drawn with Canvas.picture and saved.
Pixels are addressed by (col, row), with (0, 0) at the top left and rows growing downward, as in the image file. This is unlike a Canvas's user coordinates. Every pixel can hold any color and alpha exactly, whatever format the picture was loaded from.

Pixel coordinates are checked: col must be in 0..width-1 and row in 0..height-1, and rgb/argb must be in range, or the call fails its precondition. The transformations return a new picture and leave this one unchanged. Only set, set_rgb, set_argb and fill change a picture.
intern graphics/Picture
-- Red rises left to right, blue top to bottom.
let p := create Picture.make(256, 256)
from let row := 0 until row = 256 do
  from let col := 0 until col = 256 do
    p.set_rgb(col, row, col * 65536 + row)
    col := col + 1
  end
  row := row + 1
end
p.save("gradient.png")
-- Swap the red and blue channels of a photo.
let photo := create Picture.load("photo.jpg")
from let row := 0 until row = photo.height do
  from let col := 0 until col = photo.width do
    let c := photo.get(col, row)
    photo.set(col, row, create Color.make_rgba(c.blue, c.green, c.red, c.alpha))
    col := col + 1
  end
  row := row + 1
end
photo.grayscale().rotated_right().save("photo_gray.png")
A per-pixel loop is fine for small and medium images: on the compiled backend one get and one set per pixel over a 512x512 picture takes a second or two (grayscale is such a loop, so it costs about the same). fill, cropped, scaled and the flips and turns are done by Java2D in a single call, so they are much faster.

Example
intern io/Path

let root: Path := create Path.make("tmp")
root.create_directories()

let file: Path := root.child("notes.txt")
file.write_text("hello")
file.append_text(" world")

print(file.read_text())               -- "hello world"
print(file.name())                    -- "notes.txt"
print(file.extension())               -- "txt"
print(file.name_without_extension())  -- "notes"
print(file.size())                    -- 11
print(file.parent())                  -- tmp

file.copy_to(root.child("backup.txt"))
print(root.list().length)             -- 2

root.delete_tree()
print(root.exists())                  -- false

move_to() is implemented as a copy followed by delete_tree() of the source.
copy_to() creates missing parent directories of the target.
A leading dot does not start an extension: ".bashrc" has extension "".
Filesystem failures (missing parent directory, permission denied, reading a missing file) are raised as runtime errors.
Text I/O always uses UTF-8.

print(rx.replace("v1 v2", "#"))           -- "#1 #2"

let digits: Regex := create Regex.compile("[0-9]+")
print(digits.matches("123abc"))           -- false (whole-string match)
print(digits.find("no digits"))           -- nil

let comma: Regex := create Regex.compile(",\\s*")
print(comma.split("a, b,c"))              -- ["a", "b", "c"]

let email: Regex := create Regex.compile("(\\w+)@(\\w+)")
print(email.replace("ann@home", "$2:$1")) -- "home:ann"

title: Text Libraries
text:
Notes
find() and find_all() return the whole match, not individual capture groups.
Backslashes must be doubled inside Nex string literals: the pattern \s is written "\\s".
Compile a Regex once and reuse it; each method call applies the stored pattern and flags.

Notes
Day and week durations are fixed multiples of 24 hours; they do not account for calendar effects.
There is no month or year duration, since those vary in length.

title: Time Libraries
text:
Example
intern time/Duration
intern time/Date_Time

let start: Date_Time := create Date_Time.make(2026, 3, 13, 10, 30, 0)
let later: Date_Time := start.add(create Duration.hours(2))

print(start.format_iso())                     -- "2026-03-13T10:30:00Z"
print(start.month_name())                     -- "March"
print(start.weekday())                        -- 5
print(start.weekday_name())                   -- "Friday"
print(start.day_of_year())                    -- 72
print(start.truncate_to_day().format_iso())   -- "2026-03-13T00:00:00Z"
print(start.truncate_to_hour().format_iso())  -- "2026-03-13T10:00:00Z"
print(later.hour())                           -- 12
print(later.difference(start).total_seconds())  -- 7200.0
print(start.is_before(later))                 -- true

let local: Date_Time := create Date_Time.parse_iso("2026-03-13T12:30:00+02:00")
print(local.format_iso())                     -- "2026-03-13T10:30:00Z"

title: Time Libraries
text:
Notes
All calendar fields are computed in UTC; there is no local time zone support.
format_iso() includes fractional seconds only when they are non-zero, e.g. "1970-01-01T00:00:01.500Z".
Comparison uses is_before / is_after or epoch_millis(); equal instants are neither before nor after each other.

Http_Client is a small portable HTTP client wrapper shipped as a Nex library under lib/net/http_client.nex. Its Nex methods are implemented on top of the built-in http_get and http_post functions.

Route handlers receive Http_Request and return Http_Server_Response.
Http_Request exposes:

Arguments
Returns

Register a GET route handler.

Example
intern net/Http_Server

let server: Http_Server := create Http_Server.make(8080)

server.get("/hello/:name", fn(req: Http_Request): Http_Server_Response do
  result := create Http_Server_Response.text("hello " + req.param("name"))
end)

server.get("/search", fn(req: Http_Request): Http_Server_Response do
  result := create Http_Server_Response.text("q=" + req.query_param("q"))
end)

server.get("/files/*", fn(req: Http_Request): Http_Server_Response do
  result := create Http_Server_Response.text(req.wildcard())
end)

server.put("/items/:id", fn(req: Http_Request): Http_Server_Response do
  result := create Http_Server_Response.text("updated " + req.param("id"))
end)

server.start()
print(server.port)


Notes

Route patterns support exact paths, named parameters such as :name, and a trailing wildcard *.
Supported verbs are GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE.
Query strings are parsed into req.query() and req.query_param("name").
Route handlers are ordinary Nex function values.
The JVM interpreter and compiled code use JDK HttpServer.

net/Tcp_Socket
Tcp_Socket is a small blocking TCP client wrapper shipped as a Nex library under lib/net/tcp_socket.nex.

Loading

The loader accepts these common layouts:

~/.nex/deps/net/tcp_socket.nex



Construction
let sock: Tcp_Socket := create Tcp_Socket.make("example.com", 80)
Construction does not connect immediately. It only records the endpoint.


Methods









Method
Arguments
Returns
Description




make
host: String, port: Integer
Tcp_Socket
Create a disconnected wrapper for an endpoint.


from_socket
open_socket: Socket
Tcp_Socket
Wrap an already accepted JVM socket.

none
nil
Open the TCP connection.

Boolean
Try to connect within the timeout. Returns true on success and raises on timeout or connection failure.

none
nil
Close the connection. Safe to call repeatedly.

none
String
Return a descriptive endpoint string.





Contracts

make requires a non-empty host and a port in 1..65535
connect requires the socket to be disconnected
connect(timeout_ms) requires a non-negative timeout
send, send_line, and read_line require the socket to be connected
close guarantees the socket is disconnected on return



Example
intern net/Tcp_Socket

let sock: Tcp_Socket := create Tcp_Socket.make("example.com", 80)
sock.connect()
sock.send_line("GET / HTTP/1.0")
sock.send_line("")
print(sock.read_line())
sock.close()
Timeout-aware connect:
let sock: Tcp_Socket := create Tcp_Socket.make("example.com", 80)
if sock.connect(500) then
  print("connected")
end


Notes

This wrapper is blocking. Reads and writes wait for the underlying Java socket.
Connection failures and I/O failures are raised as runtime errors from the underlying JVM classes.
from_socket is intended for use by Server_Socket.accept.

net/Server_Socket
Server_Socket is a blocking TCP server wrapper shipped as a Nex library under lib/net/server_socket.nex.

Loading
intern net/Server_Socket
Server_Socket internally interns net/Tcp_Socket so accepted clients are returned as Tcp_Socket values.


Construction
let server: Server_Socket := create Server_Socket.make(8080)
Construction does not bind immediately. Use 0 to request an ephemeral port from the OS.


Methods









Method
Arguments
Returns
Description

Create a disconnected wrapper for a local TCP port.

Bind the server socket to the configured port.

Tcp_Socket
Block until a client connects, then return a wrapped client socket.

Tcp_Socket
Wait up to the timeout for a client. Raises on timeout or accept failure.

none
nil
Close the server socket. Safe to call repeatedly.


to_string
none
String
Return a descriptive local endpoint string.





Contracts

make requires a port in 0..65535
open requires the server socket to be closed
accept requires the server socket to be listening
accept(timeout_ms) requires a non-negative timeout
close guarantees the server socket is closed on return



Example
intern net/Server_Socket

let server: Server_Socket := create Server_Socket.make(8080)
server.open()
let client: Tcp_Socket := server.accept()
client.send_line("hello")
client.close()
server.close()
Timeout-aware accept:
let server: Server_Socket := create Server_Socket.make(8080)
server.open()
let client: Tcp_Socket := server.accept(1000)
client.send_line("hello")
client.close()
server.close()


Notes

This wrapper is blocking. accept waits for an incoming connection.
If make(0) is used, open updates port to the actual OS-assigned port.
Connection failures, timeouts, and I/O failures are raised as runtime errors from the underlying JVM classes.
